title: Starkman: GM CEO Mary Barra’s ‘Betting on America’ Begins with Next-Gen Pickups Built in Mexico
readable_text:
The writer, a Los Angeles freelancer and former Detroit News business reporter, writes a blog, Starkman Approved .

By Eric Starkman

I’ve come to grudgingly admire GM CEO Mary Barra’s ability to get away with her unabashed audacity.

AI-generated satirical illustration that reads: "Thank you Ms. Barra, for betting on us."

In what amounts to a giant FU to President Trump and the UAW, GM has reportedly chosen its assembly plant in Silao, Mexico, to initiate production on Oct. 12 of its next-generation 2027 Chevy Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 pickups, the crown jewels on whose future GM’s profitability rests. The trucks will arrive packed with software and new powertrains that supposedly justify their stratospheric sticker prices.

Although Ford is undeniably more red, white, and blue, GM in June 2025 issued a self-congratulatory news release headlined “Betting on America,” claiming it would invest $4 billion in U.S. manufacturing over the next two years. The release featured this mint Barra quote:

“We believe the future of transportation will be driven by American innovation and manufacturing expertise ,” Barra said. The investment, she added, “demonstrates our ongoing commitment to build vehicles in the U.S. and to support American jobs.”

Perhaps Barra meant North American jobs.

Given that the Trump administration just awarded GM Defense a nearly $700 million expansion of its military vehicle contract, while Trump’s Transportation Secretary publicly and unfairly hammered Ford over its Chinese ties , one might expect Barra to judiciously avoid the appearance of undermining the administration’s industrial agenda. Instead, choosing Silao to handle the initial rollout of the next-gen Silverados and Sierras is an unmistakable slap in the face to UAW workers in Fort Wayne, Ind., who won’t begin building the new models until early 2027.

The UAW routinely urges Americans to check vehicle VINs to determine country of origin; any number beginning with a “3” means Mexican-built. Despite Barra’s patriotic chest-thumping, she is clearly betting that her considerably lower-paid Mexican workforce can handle the critical Silverado and Sierra launches just as well as, or better than, union hands in Indiana.

Backbone of Detroit 3

The move cuts directly to the core of the UAW’s product allocation security. Full-size pickups are the financial backbone of the Detroit Three. Handing the lead launch slot for GM’s most important and profitable vehicle franchise to Mexico signals that GM is fully prepared to dilute domestic leverage whenever a major platform transition presents an opening.

Further underscoring that the chutzpah of Barra’s GM knows no bounds, the trade publication GM Authority also reports that General Motors South America has just declared its embattled Alvear plant in Argentina part of the company’s long-term growth strategy.

“The GM Automotive Complex in Alvear holds a strategic position within General Motors’ South American operations,” insisted Thomas Owsianski, who was appointed President and Managing Director of GM South America in January.

It’s a brave corporate face on a hush-toned reality: across Latin America, GM has largely surrendered vehicle development to China. The models GM markets across the region under the Chevy bowtie are overwhelmingly engineered and built by its Chinese joint-venture partners. In fact, to bypass Mexico’s steep tariffs on vehicles imported directly from China, GM is now preparing to assemble Chinese-engineered Chevrolet models inside Mexico.

Making America Great Again

Trump wants to Make America Great Again. The profit margins of Mary Barra’s General Motors are borderless. The company’s most affordable vehicles are manufactured in South Korea, where GM maintains a major production operation.

That same borderless opportunism defines Barra’s environmental record.

In 2019, when Barra killed the plug-in Chevy Volt, arguably among the most innovative vehicles in GM’s history, she told investors that “customers generally aren’t interested in hybrids” and vowed an all-electric crusade to save the planet. She famously pledged that GM was on a path to an all-EV future by 2035.

Barra’s GM is singing an entirely different tune these days. Reuters reported that GM enthusiastically backed the Trump administration’s dramatic rollback of vehicle fuel economy mandates, praising its “intention to better align fuel economy standards with market realities.”

The Transportation Department estimates that the revised mandate will save GM a staggering $20.4 billion in technology costs through 2031. Barra’s environmental piety evaporated the moment deregulation offered a multi-billion-dollar reprieve to GM’s bottom line.

According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s 2025 Automotive Trends Report , GM’s fleet averaged just 22.9 miles per gallon in the 2024 model year, placing the company near the bottom of the industry. Stellantis performed a tad worse, at 22.8 mpg.

The industry average was 27.2 mpg; GM trails the broader market by more than four miles per gallon. GM claims on its website that it is “leading the charge toward zero tailpipe emissions.”
